title: Esther 1:10–12
context: On the seventh day of the people’s feast, when the king’s heart is merry with wine, he sends seven eunuchs to bring Vashti the queen before him wearing the royal crown, to show the people and the princes her beauty. She refuses to come at the commandment, and the king’s anger burns. The text states the command, the refusal, and the anger; it does not give Vashti’s reasons, and the notes do not invent them. The scene should be handled soberly, without speculation about the summons and without turning Vashti into a modern symbol, whether of defiance or of failure. The book still does not name God. A later providence reading, that her refusal opens the way for another queen, is common in both traditions and may be named as a reading of the story’s shape, hedged, not as a hidden message in this refusal itself. Both traditions treat the unit as the narrative turning point of the chapter, a royal command refused and a court thrown into anger, without a party contrast over Vashti’s motive.

verses.text: On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcass, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king,
verses.arminianNotes:
On the seventh day, “when the heart of the king was merry with wine,” he commands seven eunuchs who serve in his presence: Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcass. The names are given as a court list. The king’s merriment with wine is the stated condition of the command that follows, and the notes do not go beyond that into a portrait of drunkenness the verse does not draw at length.

Arminian readers take the seventh day and the merry heart as the real setting of the summons, a historical moment in the feast, not a fable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the wine and the seven servants as the narrative’s own explanation of how the command was sent, a court acting in the midst of the banquet.

Both traditions refuse to sensationalize the merriment, and they invent no contrast over the eunuchs’ names.

verses.text: to bring Vashti the queen before the king wearing the royal crown, to show the people and the princes her beauty; for she was beautiful.
verses.arminianNotes:
The eunuchs are to “bring Vashti the queen before the king wearing the royal crown, to show the people and the princes her beauty; for she was beautiful.” The stated purpose is display: her beauty is to be shown in the royal crown before the people and the princes. The verse does not add further detail about how she was to appear, and the notes do not supply it.

Arminian readers take the command as a real royal order to bring the queen into the public feast, an order about beauty and display, reported without prurience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stay with what is written: the queen is to come wearing the royal crown, so that her beauty may be shown. Motives beyond that display are not given.

Both traditions handle the summons soberly and refuse to turn it into a modern culture-war example, or into a coded sign.

verses.text: But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king’s commandment by the eunuchs. Therefore the king was very angry, and his anger burned in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king’s commandment by the eunuchs. Therefore the king was very angry, and his anger burned in him.” The refusal is stated without an explanation from Vashti. The king’s anger is the immediate result, and it will drive the counsel of the next unit. Readers have long offered reasons for the refusal; this verse does not, and the notes leave the gap as a gap.

Arminian readers take the refusal as a real, costly act at court, and they refuse either to condemn or to celebrate Vashti beyond what the narrative itself will do.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the two facts the verse gives: she would not come, and the king’s anger burned. The later shape of the book, in which her removal opens a place for Esther, may be noted as a common providence reading of the whole, not as a secret meaning packed into this line.

Both traditions treat the turning point soberly, without a contrast over Vashti’s heart, and without claiming to know why she refused.
